svg.title: The three multi-agent topologies: sequential, fan-out and fan-in, and supervisor
svg.desc: A hand-drawn comparison of three wirings. The first, a sequential pipeline, shows three boxes A, B, and C joined left to right, each stage with one job; it fits clear hand-offs such as parse then analyse then format, risks end-to-end latency because every step is serial, and is auditable because each stage logs its own input and output. The second, fan-out and fan-in, shows a parent splitting to three parallel workers and rejoining at a reducer; it fits doing one thing for each of many items, its latency is the slowest worker, its cost scales linearly, and the reducer is where most bugs hide. The third, supervisor and worker, shows a supervisor with two-way arrows to three workers, deciding turn by turn; it fits problems where the decomposition is itself the work, and risks the supervisor doing the job inside its own context while the workers go decorative. Captions note the first two are workflows and the third is an agent, and advise starting with the workflows.
svg.text: Three wirings account for almost every production multi-agent system. Two are workflows; one is an agent.

Sequential and fan-out are workflows: the engineer writes the control flow. The supervisor is an agent: the model picks the next step.
Start with sequential or fan-out. Reach for a supervisor only when the decomposition genuinely cannot be planned ahead.
